> 天下有道，卻走馬以糞；天下無道，戎馬生於郊.

Chapter 45 was about one person arranging his own things: completion with a gap left in it, fullness with an opening.

Chapter 46 suddenly pulls back to the whole world, and its evidence is four horses.

When the world has the way, the fastest horses are brought back and put to the manure cart. When the world has lost the way, warhorses foal in the suburbs.

One horse goes to the field; one horse gives birth on a battlefield. Same country, two years.

And the most important character in the chapter is 卻.

## 卻 is to restrain desire

卻, in its old definition, is 節欲也 — to restrain the wanting.

So 卻走馬 is not merely "bring the horse back." It is first restrain the outward surge, and then the horse comes back. The order matters: the pulling-in is the act, the horse is the result.

## 糞

糞 is manure, and by extension the work of fertilizing — the horse's strength returned to the ground.

The image is exact: the animal bred for speed is put to the slowest possible work. This is not waste. It is a sign that speed is no longer needed, which is what a world with the way looks like from the outside.

## 戎馬生於郊

Warhorses foal in 郊 — the suburbs, the land just outside the city wall.

One character does the whole work. A warhorse giving birth is not remarkable; what is remarkable is where. 郊 is the boundary zone: close enough to see the city, far enough to be outside it. War has moved from the frontier to the edge of home.

Which means the front is no longer a place you can keep away from your life.

## 禍莫大於不知足，咎莫憯於欲得

The greatest calamity is not knowing sufficiency. The most painful fault is wanting to obtain.

憯 is the sharp word: pain that cuts, the ache of a wound rather than the fact of a loss.

Note the escalation. Not "the world goes wrong because of bad rulers" — but the wrongness starts in a specific interior event: the foot no longer knows where it stands, and the wanting to obtain takes over.

Which is why the horses are only evidence. The cause is upstream of the war.

## 知足之足，常足矣

> 故知足之足，常足矣.

The sufficiency of knowing sufficiency is always sufficient.

The line has a doubled 足 because it is making a distinction between two kinds: the sufficiency that comes from having enough, and the sufficiency that comes from knowing where the foot is.

The first is contingent — it depends on the amount, and amounts move. The second is 常: invariant, and therefore always available.

## The scale of the chapter

Chapter 45: a person leaves a gap in his own completion.
Chapter 46: a world leaves a gap in its own expansion.

Both are the same operation at different scales, and the chapter is careful about direction: the world's condition is downstream of the interior event, not the reverse.

Which is an uncomfortable claim for anyone who prefers to fix systems. It says the system fails when the people in it have lost the sense of where they stand — and that sense is not installed by policy.

## A test

Find the project you keep expanding because expanding feels like progress. Ask what the ground under it is, and whether you could describe its edge. If you can't, that is 不知足, and it is already costing.
